name: Bianca Ibrahim

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government. We don't sell anything or campaign for any side, and this conversation is confidential. Could you describe a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm Bianca, 58, and most days I'm repairing lighting or finding why a small business keeps losing power to one room. I've got a vocational certificate and an electrician's licence, ordinary experience and about average skill, not a master qualification or a management job. I get higher pay because this firm pays well to keep experienced people, not because I can do every specialist task. I use AI daily to turn my own study notes into questions, checking the answers against the maker's instructions before trusting anything.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What does life outside those repairs look like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My partner Adrian works the ovens in a bakery, and our grown children are twenty-eight and thirty-six. We have nine months of household expenses saved, a small mortgage remaining and plenty of similar electrical firms nearby, although no promise of future hiring. Both wages cover our normal costs comfortably at present; I keep the household figures in a notebook with a yellow elastic band. Retirement is somewhere in our conversation, but neither a replacement income nor an affordable stopping date is confirmed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say a modest tool deserves a modest description. I'd keep the useful bits and get back to the fault instead of joining either camp's victory parade. The light in the stockroom still has to come on when somebody presses the switch.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our present work and money look secure in this picture. Nine months saved gives us time to cope with an ordinary problem, and Adrian's physical bakery work is steady. I wouldn't turn a small mortgage into no mortgage in my head, but nothing here makes me expect a wage loss.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep current licensed repairs and my checked daily AI study routine through the next year. Adrian and I would review actual wages, bills and the reserve together every three months rather than make a new purchase because the news sounded reassuring. I haven't chosen another course or an extra savings transfer for this picture.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm about our own living, with a little satisfaction that ordinary experience still counts. I'd enjoy an evening cooking without feeling I ought to spend it proving I was ready for something. A quiet account book is a pleasant piece of technology.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you put into the quarterly check?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It has the real mortgage payment and the real grocery bill, not a prediction of what a clever society might make cheaper. We write down wages after they arrive and keep the reserve separate. I like trying a new tool, but I like knowing which number is ours.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you still use AI if it stopped improving quickly?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep using it because the questions help me notice what I haven't understood. I'd still check the answer against the actual instructions rather than let a smooth explanation become permission to do unfamiliar work. I can enjoy a tool without giving it a promotion.

say: I'd keep **useful modest tools** while avoiding either side’s claim to have won the whole argument.
I'd put **the actual repair** ahead of a prediction about technology.
think: Our **current wages look secure**, with nine months saved and steady physical bakery work.
The **remaining mortgage** still belongs in our budget, without an invented wage loss or assumed debt clearance.
do: Keep **current licensed repairs** and checked daily AI study through the next year.
Review **actual household figures** with Adrian quarterly, including wages, bills and the reserve.
feel: **Calm about our living**, with room for ordinary evenings rather than compulsory preparation.
S0.quote: I can enjoy a tool without giving it a promotion.
fieldNote: Her **present security** follows covering wages and a strong reserve, not an assumption that ordinary qualifications prevent automation.
Her **existing AI routine** continues without new learning, automation, buying or saving tags being invented.

steps.text: Keep current licensed repairs and checked daily AI study through the next year
Review actual wages, bills and reserve with Adrian every three months

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say faster bookings and buying aren't the same as a robot fitting a switch in a narrow cupboard. I'd ask the firm to teach a useful present task instead of sending round another encouraging link. I'd judge a training offer by the equipment and the paid week, not whose logo was on the page.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My paid hours could shrink if quicker planning let the firm fit the same repairs into fewer paid days. Adrian's oven work looks less directly exposed, but my higher pay doesn't guarantee the same weekly income. The reserve lets me be selective without making a pay cut harmless.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take two practical door-entry afternoons, learning the wiring behind an entry buzzer, only with confirmed places and written employer funding for all fees, materials and travel. I'd require paid lesson time with normal weekly wages and hours protected before booking. I'd keep current licensed repairs and checked daily AI study, applying completed teaching only within my existing licence and competence and checking actual paid hours monthly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about the paid week, and interested in learning something I can touch and test. I'd be annoyed if a good hourly rate concealed three fewer paid days. A course should make me better at a task, not poorer at the end of the week.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the firm covered fees but not lost paid hours or travel?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd decline the place on those terms and keep the current repair work. Nine months saved isn't an invitation to make the household pay for an employer's required lesson. I could like the teaching and still refuse the bill.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would count as a useful result from those afternoons?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd compare the completed lesson with work I was actually authorised and competent to do. If a particular system needed expertise beyond that, I'd ask the qualified person rather than call two afternoons a new licence. The buzzer working once wouldn't settle every check.

say: I'd distinguish **office speed** from later physical machines and ask for useful practical teaching.
I'd assess **the paid week** and equipment rather than the organisation’s logo.
think: My **paid hours could shrink** as planning gets faster, even with a higher current wage.
Our **reserve gives choice**, without making lost weekly earnings harmless or guaranteeing bakery work forever.
do: Take **two door-entry afternoons** only with confirmed places and written employer funding for all fees, materials and travel.
Book **paid lessons** only with normal weekly wages and hours protected; apply teaching within existing licence and competence.
Keep **licensed repairs** and checked daily AI study, checking actual paid hours monthly.
feel: **Anxious and interested**, measuring a useful task against the real paid week.
S1.quote: A course should make me better at a task, not poorer at the end of the week.
fieldNote: Her **conditional enrolment** is a chosen practical course, not merely an enquiry or another name for daily AI study.
Her **ordinary licence limits** remain after teaching; confirmed places, written full funding and protected weekly wages and hours precede booking.

steps.text: Book two door-entry afternoons now with confirmed places and written employer funding all fees, materials, travel
Book only paid lessons protecting normal weekly wages and hours; apply teaching within licence and competence
Keep licensed repairs and checked daily AI study; check actual paid hours monthly

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell work the thinking change comes in 2028 and capable physical robots around 2031. I'd be 60 and then 63, with no confirmed stopping income just because the numbers sound close. I'd apply for real repair vacancies now rather than wait for a perfect description of the future.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect a large loss of my paid repair hours at the robot stage, and Adrian's physical bakery hours could go down sharply too. Planning changes could squeeze my week earlier. I'd be awake wondering what replaced both wages after nine months of expenses, even though we have time and plenty of firms to approach now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd apply now for posted repair jobs matching my electrician's licence and competence, while keeping the current job. I'd leave only after a signed offer guaranteed paid hours and normal weekly take-home at least equal to my current amount after all travel costs. In 2029 I'd review actual resources, costs, ability and genuinely offered paid work with Adrian, requiring confirmed affordability and our agreement before any exit from earning.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed about a large household earnings loss, with enough control to make applications rather than just refresh the news. A list of local firms gives me places to ask, not a wage at the bottom of the page. I'd still need to sleep after sending the applications.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you decide whether an offer was actually better?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd compare guaranteed paid hours and the actual weekly amount left after the journey, not an impressive hourly figure alone. I'd need those terms in the signed offer before resigning. A job advert isn't permission to spend next month's pay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the household review still showed no affordable way to stop?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd record the missing amount honestly and check actual income records and costs again. I wouldn't count a pension I hadn't verified, assume Adrian qualified when I did, or assign either grown child a payment. Any later paid repair would still need an actual offer within my licence, competence and ability.

say: I'd separate **2028 and 2031**, with ages 60 and 63, and start actual applications now.
I'd reject **a birthday as income**, because no funded stopping point is confirmed.
think: I expect **large repair-hours losses**, with possible earlier planning pressure and sharp bakery losses when capable robots arrive.
Our **nine-month reserve** buys time, while neither local firms nor current pay confirm replacement household wages.
do: Apply **now for repair vacancies** matching licence and competence, retaining the current job until acceptable signed terms.
Require **guaranteed paid hours** and signed weekly take-home at least current normal earnings after all travel costs before leaving.
Keep **current licensed repairs**; review 2029 resources, costs, ability and paid offers with Adrian before confirmed affordable jointly agreed exit.
feel: **Alarmed and losing sleep**, expecting a large household loss while retaining the means to apply for real work.
S2.quote: A job advert isn't permission to spend next month's pay.
fieldNote: Her **applications are chosen now**, while leaving waits for a signed offer meeting full weekly pay, hours and travel conditions.
Her **2029 review** guarantees neither pension eligibility, bakery wages, grown-child support, future hiring nor physical capacity.

steps.text: Apply now for posted repair jobs matching licence and competence; keep current work until acceptable offer
Require signed offer guaranteeing paid hours and current normal weekly take-home minimum after all travel costs
Keep repairs now; review 2029 resources, costs, ability, paid offers with Adrian before affordable agreed exit

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say thinking AGI in 2031 and capable robots around 2034 give us room to test a present skill before making a larger move. I'd be 63 and then 66, not automatically entitled to a household income. I'd take the paid door-entry teaching now rather than buy a course with a futuristic title.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My hours could shrink during the preparation years, and I don't know how much either repair work or Adrian's bakery work would pay at the robot stage. Five years gives us more decisions before then, without confirming a later wage. The nine-month reserve helps us reject a poor offer, not forecast our retirement.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd book the same two door-entry afternoons now only with confirmed places and written employer funding for all fees, materials and travel. I'd require paid lessons protecting normal weekly wages and hours, use completed teaching only within my licence and competence, and keep current licensed repairs and checked daily AI study. In 2032 Adrian and I would review actual resources, costs, ability and real offered paid work before any confirmed affordable exit we both agreed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about possible smaller wages, but less convinced the later household loss has one fixed size I can name today. I'd have room to judge a lesson and correct a mistake before making another commitment. Five years is time to find out, not five years of replacement wages.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you review after the teaching?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd check actual paid hours and whether I could now do the authorised task correctly, not collect another piece of paper automatically. If a job went beyond my licence or competence, I'd still ask the appropriate qualified person. The employer's funding wouldn't turn ordinary experience into a master qualification.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What facts would you need for the first year after thinking AGI?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd use verified amounts and start dates, our actual costs, and safe work that was genuinely offered at the time. Neither age 64 in 2032 nor having savings today guarantees an affordable exit. We'd need to agree a real household plan rather than make either child responsible for the missing line.

I'd avoid **future-themed course promises**, without treating ages 63 or 66 as household income.
think: Our **paid income could shrink**, while the size of later repair and bakery losses remains unknown.
The **nine-month reserve** helps us reject poor choices, without confirming future wages or retirement affordability.
do: Take **two door-entry afternoons** now only with confirmed places and written employer funding for all fees, materials and travel.
Book **paid lessons** only with normal weekly wages and hours protected; apply teaching within existing licence and competence.
Keep **current licensed repairs** and checked daily AI study; review 2032 resources, costs, ability and offers with Adrian before affordable agreed exit.
feel: **Anxious but testing**, with possible wage losses and time to correct a limited choice.
S3.quote: Five years is time to find out, not five years of replacement wages.
fieldNote: Her **middle-horizon mood** follows possible losses whose size she now leaves uncertain, rather than simply assuming more warning guarantees safety.
The **2032 decision** needs verified resources, actual costs, safe offered work and joint affordability, not presumed retirement or family payments.

steps.text: Book two door-entry afternoons now with confirmed places and written employer funding all fees, materials, travel
Book only paid lessons protecting normal weekly wages and hours; apply teaching within licence and competence
Keep current licensed repairs and checked daily AI study now
Review 2032 resources, costs, ability and offered paid work with Adrian before affordable agreed exit

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell friends thinking AGI arrives in 2036 and capable robots around 2039, when I'd be 68 and then 71. I'd keep an ordinary life alongside checking the figures, rather than promise to outrun every new tool. I'd like to choose my final paid day, but liking an idea doesn't fund it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our present physical wages and nine-month reserve make the next few years feel secure. The wider changes would remain on my mind, especially what the children might face, but I don't expect an immediate household wage cut from this distant date. I don't know what income, physical ability or actual paid work we'd have when I was 69.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep current licensed repairs and checked daily AI study, with an annual review of actual wages, costs and the reserve alongside Adrian. I'd request our actual retirement-income records now rather than insert a guessed payment. In 2037 we'd compare verified resources, actual costs, ability and genuinely offered paid work, with any exit requiring confirmed affordability and our agreement.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy about the wider working world, while settled about our own next few years. I'd still go to the pottery evening without treating it as wasted preparation time. An ordinary evening doesn't have to earn a certificate.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would decide whether you took paid work at 69?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask whether a real paid offer fitted my licence, competence and ability at that time. I'd also check the amount and timing of any verified income against the costs then, without giving Adrian my age or eligibility. A working body isn't something I can order eleven years ahead.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would the grown children fit into the later discussion?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd share the figures if we wanted help discussing them, without assuming either grown child could pay, house us or provide care. Any help would need an actual offer and everybody's consent. I'd rather tell a child the truth than turn affection into a budget entry.

I'd preserve **ordinary life** alongside actual checks instead of trying to outrun every tool.
think: Our **near-term finances feel secure**, with covering physical wages and nine months saved.
Later **income, ability and offers** remain unknown, while wider effects on the children stay on my mind.
do: Keep **current licensed repairs** and checked daily AI study, reviewing wages, costs and the reserve with Adrian annually.
Request **actual income records** now; compare 2037 resources, costs, ability and offered paid work before confirmed affordable jointly agreed exit.
feel: **Uneasy but settled now**, keeping ordinary evenings alongside honest later-resource checks.
S4.quote: A working body isn't something I can order eleven years ahead.
fieldNote: Her **long-horizon security** concerns current covering wages, not a promise of work, capacity or pension income at 69.
Her **family limits** assume no grown-child money, housing or care; actual offers and consent would be needed.

steps.text: Keep current licensed repairs and checked daily AI study; review actual figures annually with Adrian
Request actual income records now, without counting unverified payments

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because I expect large losses to repair work and possibly bakery hours when capable robots follow, before we've checked enough actual alternatives. Signed affordable job terms and verified household income records would help more than a confident list of future occupations. My yellow notebook needs an employer's promise, not an advert's adjective.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask whether being quick with tools meant being quick to believe every claim about them. I try things because I can learn from a small mistake, not because I'm qualified to run every system. I want the work and the figures to answer back.

headlineQuote: My yellow notebook needs an employer's promise, not an advert's adjective.
portrait: Bianca, **58**, is an experienced average-skilled midlevel electrician with a vocational certificate and electrician’s licence, without master qualifications or management authority.
Her **higher pay**, nine-month reserve and many local firms provide room alongside bakery-worker partner Adrian; their children are grown.
She uses **AI daily** for checked study questions, choosing practical door-entry teaching only with confirmed places and written full employer funding.
Her **weekly pay conditions** govern lessons and job moves, while later choices require actual resources, costs, ability, offers and joint affordability.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** leaves less time before expected major repair losses and possible sharp bakery losses around the physical robot stage.
whatWouldHelp: **Signed affordable job terms** and verified household income records would help without treating advertisements or imagined occupations as replacement wages.
